Respecting the dead

By: Annalise Lubbe | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Meet two rather unusual people: Christopher Fitchet from the Southern Cape and Eugene Liebenberg from Gauteng, both paying homage to the dead by visiting their graves.

Unique Selling Point:
Christopher had a burning desire to trace the origin of his rather unusual family name and Eugene, still haunted by the ghosts of the border war, to pay homage to the fallen brothers in arms.


Summary:
Christopher Fitchet’s mission began 8 years ago when he searched for his ancestors. Even though the surname is uncommon, few documents were available on the family tree. He turned to the cemeteries across the country in the hope of finding family graves: his search took him from the Eastern Cape to the Free State and all the way down to the Western Cape, photographing every single Fitchet gravestone and documenting the family tree. It turned out there were 1500 South African family members with that surname (Pretorius is about 200 000 in comparison). He traced his founding mother, Mary-Anne Collison, born in England and his Founding father from Calcutta who ended up in South Africa when their ship landed in the Cape in 1817.

During this mission to document the graves of the ancestors he noticed the state of neglect of the graves in cemeteries across the country and that is ‘when the penny dropped’ said Christopher. I had to photograph every single grave in the cemetery as a method of preserving the dead as tomorrow it might not be there any more. In some instances the burial register is gone which means if the graves are destroyed the dead will forever disappear in living history.

From the caretakers he heard stories of people removing the headstones to sell, others were digging for jewelry in the boxes as they believe it is buried with the deceased, and the worst is stealing the ashes of the dead to mix with street drugs like Nyaope. In Bloemfontein he spent 4 days picking up ashes and putting the memorial plaques back again - including those of his family buried there.

Christopher’s passion to preserve the history of the dead has resulted in over 350 000 photos taken of the graves in many towns, cities and even on farms. The photos are then donated to the Genealogical Society of South Africa’s Gravestone Photos Project and available on their website for anyone searching for a family member.

There are a number of organisations focusing on documenting graves, but none were focusing on the rural areas and the farms so this became his focus over the last 3 years. For Christopher this is a way of giving back because life is not just about taking, he says.

Over the years he has met very interesting people and places like Uniondale known for its ghost of a lonely young woman who hitches a ride and then when people offer her a lift, she gets into the car and then simply vanishes. The ghost, known as Maria Roux, was a young woman who tragically died in the early hours of 12 April 1968 when her fiance lost control of the car in which they were travelling. He visited the farm nearby the exact place where the accident happened and it was a strange eerie feeling, he remembered.

Christopher’s next photographic grave project is Swellendam in the Western Cape, a historic town established in 1745 named after Governor Hendrik Swellengrebel and his wife Helena ten DammeIt. There are over 50 provincial heritage sites, 4 cemeteries, and a large number of farm graves in the district.

Eugene Liebenberg’s story is rather different: Having fought in the border war he pays homage to the fallen soldiers in Operation Askari and Operation Sceptic, also known as Operation Smokeshell. He finds the grave sites from the records on the South African War Graves project, whose aim is to archive photographs from South African and Rhodesian wars. He then locates the graves to pay homage. He found most of the soldiers’ graves neglected, overgrown and unsafe to visit.

“Some graves, like the ones in Boksburg cemetery, are so overgrown that I spend hours clearing my way through the weeds in search of the graves”, says Eugene. “It takes hours sometimes and I can’t believe that no-one cuts the lawn and keeps the place clean”, says Eugene.

After clearing the site around the grave, Eugene cleans the dust from the headstone and places a small bunch of flowers on the grave as an act of respect and remembrance. He then takes a moment of silence to remember the fallen soldier. In a symbolic act of honouring the soldier and their journey in the afterlife he drinks a toast to angels as a way of acknowledging their presence in the world of spirits and offering respect to their guardian angel.

Eugene has struggled to come to terms with the war he had a part in - not of his own choice - and this he feels is a way of finding peace and remembering the brothers who did not make it alive, says Eugene.

For Eugene it is a matter of finding closure on a war he did not choose, paying his last respect. For Christopher every roadtrip to a forgotten cemetery on a farm or a town or a hamlet is a journey back into the past where he painstakingly captures frame by frame a tombstone of a family member creating a “window to the past”, etched in memory. And for those who cannot get to the graves, being able to see their loved ones' burial site online is a special feeling, says Christopher.

Riana Le Roux manages the Photographic Grave Project on the Genealogical Society of South Africa’s website. She spent a decade cataloguing and posting hundreds of thousands of photographs from graves in South Africa and neighbouring countries on the website for viewers to find at the click of a button. The search engine is easy to navigate. All graves that have been photographed and sent to Riana will be available online. By simply entering the name and surname of a loved one and the province where the person was buried, the photo of the grave and exact location will be displayed on the screen. “We are constantly updating our site and are thankful for people like Christopher who dedicate their spare time on taking photos for those who cannot get to the grave, and some people who live far away and are not able to go to the cemetery to pay respect”, says Riana.

We will conduct a zoom interview with Riana who lives in Baberton; spend a day with Eugene in Boksburg at the local cemetery and a day with Chrisotopher at cemeteries in Swellendam. In addition we have graves from cemeteries in the Northern Cape and Ceres, taken by our cameraman when he travelled through that area.

ADDITIONAL VISUALS:
Photos from Eugene in his army days; photos from an ex soldier who served on the border and kindly made his own photos available; plus 50 seconds of licensed film footage, purchased from Peter Lamberti, a professional filmmaker, to ‘set the mood’ of the Border War. On the Fitchet family, we have photographs of the graves Christopher managed to find plus a family tree graphic to illustrate the genealogy and family line dating back to the ‘Stam moeder” / matriarch.
All photos on the Photographic War Project is available for us to download.

Script:


FINAL Script: Living Memory
Duration: 10 minutes 22 seconds
Date: 21 May 2025

INTRO SLOMO SHOTS

UPSOUND CHRISTOPHER: You need to know where you come from in order to understand where you are going to…..And the starting point wasn’t with your birth. It goes back.

UPSOUND EUGENE: When I go find a grave and there is another soldier, I don’t care what colour, what kind, whatever. Blood is red.

LINK: There’s a story behind every grave, every tombstone…. It’s like opening a window into the past…you never know what you will find.

VO1
We follow two very different people on their paths of discovery:
A veteran from Gauteng, haunted by the ghosts of the Angola Border War….
and a family man from the Southern Cape with an intense longing to find his family roots.

Christopher Fitchet: I started on this journey a couple of years ago to try and identify my ancestors and where they came from and at the time I didn’t realise the whirlwind romance relationship I would have with it. It has taken me to places I never thought I would never see.

VO2
For Christopher Fitchet, the catalyst was the loss of his twins, born prematurely.

Christopher Fitchet: Part of the problem was that we were not allowed to bury our children because of the legislation at the time, and that made me think well if there is no grave for them and there is a grave for me, their existence would never be known. They would remain unknown as though they never existed.

VO3
A Grave is a sign that there was life and there was death……
For Eugene Liebenberg, it was the ghosts of the past that haunted him.

Eugene Liebenberg: There’s about 2000 people that was killed in the border war, just on our side.

LINK
Between the 1960’s and 1990’s thousands of mostly white South Africans were conscripted to fight on the South African border…. You could defer it, but you couldn’t escape it.

Up sound helicopter

VO4
Unless they were conscientious objectors, all young men did compulsory military service. The Apartheid Government used conscription to combat threats of communism and African nationalism.

Pause
Eugene was only 18 when he was called up.

He served in a unit under Operation Askari, a large-scale SADF operation into Angola to fight the military wing of the South West Africa People’s Orginasation, SWAPO and prevent a planned incursion into South West Africa.

V/O 5
24 Soldiers died in Operation Askari ... .One of them was his friend, Corporal Johannes Hendrik Roets, known as Roetsie.

Eugene Liebenberg: Man he was a kind ouk. He was one of the section leaders, he was nogal vris and he had a good sense of humour.

Govan Whittles: Did you struggle to adjust to civilian life?

Eugene Liebenberg: Unknowingly so. Because remember, all your buddies that didn’t go to the army were studying, were jolling. We were killing people.

Govan Whittles: Jees…

Eugene: You understand. Or you got killed. Get the bodies in body bags and ‘poef’, picked up by the chopper and they’re gone. And they get buried and whatever and we never see them again.

VO6
After the war, Eugene closed himself off from the army - until one day he found himself at Roetsie’s grave in Thabazimbi. That was when his search of the graves of soldiers he knew began.

Eugene: Something just fired me up, you understand, and I just went for it relentlessly. I just carried on in proper infantry style. I just went.

VO7
In honour of their memory, Eugene cleaned the graves and sent the photos to the South Africa War Graves Project website where families can visit their loved ones on a virtual platform.

Fade to black



VO8
Christopher’s burning desire to find his ancestors took him to the far corners of the globe.

Christopher Fitchet: My first ancestor was David Alexander Fitchet, he was born in Scotland and he was part of the 72nd royal regiment. They were part of the invasion of Blauberg against the Dutch government at the time at the Cape. Then he was sent to India. In India he then met his wife Mary Anne Collison, they got married at Fort William in Calcutta.

VO9
It was in Fort William’s garrison in Calcutta that he found the marriage certificate of David Alexander Fitchet and Mary Ann Collison.

Govan Whittles: Describe that moment where you researched someone on paper and found the cemetery where they’re buried. Did you find that connection that you wanted?

Christopher Fitchet: Absolutely. Mary-ann Collison is as they say in Afrikaans the ‘stam moeder’ of all Fitchets in SA and she’s buried in Bedford cemetery in the Eastern Cape. And I stumbled on this grave and I looked at this name and I thought to myself, but YOU are the reason I am here.

LINK
When we think about family trees we think about commonality, the common ground that’s shared between all of us. But family trees are also about the stories that are unique to each person, to your mother, your father, your grandmother, great grandmother, even the ‘stam moeder’, and that’s what connects us.

VO10
Christopher found 1500 Fitchets in the family tree….sadly some of their graves were badly neglected.

Govan: What condition did you find the Bedford cemetery?

Christopher: Overgrown, completely vandalised. In Bloemfontein for example I stumbled among one of my ancestors' ashes lying on the floor. I would say about 80% of the wall was completely vandalised, all the boxes were lying on the floor. We basically went puzzle building is what I called it where we tried to locate all the pieces that had been smashed and put them back together again. Ok you’re back there where you belong.

VO11
A grave is a place of remembrance…a place to connect.
Christopher Fitchet: I took my children to my grandparent’s graves….…there’s that connection. It's a sense of belonging. It's not about you and your parents and your children, that you actually belong to something a lot greater.

VO12
These photographs may help others draw their family trees as well. Christopher has donated them to the Gravestone Photo Project, run by the Genealogical Society of South Africa. On this website, people can search for lost graves of their loved ones.

Riana Le Roux: Many of the cemeteries are not accessible any more and they are being destroyed so we will have a photograph at least for posterity, some sort of record of the person who was buried there, many burial records disappear.

VO13
Riana le Roux has been cataloguing over one million photographs taken by volunteers like Chrstopher to serve as a national asset for families in search of family graves.

Govan Whittles: How did you get involved in the project?

Riana le Roux: Coordinator: Gravestone Photo Project - As a child we used to go to the Westpark cemetery quite often. It was a family tradition, Christmas Day. As I grew older I never lost my love for cemeteries. A lot of us, especially genealogists, we just love cemeteries.

Govan Whittles: Why do you think people are interested in genealogy?

Riana le Roux: Personally I think it is nice to know your roots where you came from. I find people who are, people for instance who are adopted, there is always a question, who am I? Where did I come from, where do I belong? So I think genealogy gives you the answers.

UP SOUND MUSIC

VO14
Finding the graves of fallen soldiers has brought back powerful memories for Eugene ….today will be his last.

UPSOUND: Govan Whittles: I cant’ believe how overgrown this place is.

Eugene Liebenberg: It’s unreal Govan ... .very, very, sad hey.

Govan Whittles: Do you come here alone?

Eugene Liebenberg: No not always hey. This youngster, my ‘handskind’, came with me and he helped me find about 9 graves over the years and then he does the spanner work. We share it a bit.
Govan (laughs)
Eugene: Yeah.
Govan: Lekker hey.
Eugene: He also plays the bagpipes.
Govan: The bagpipes?
Eugene: Yeah.

UPSOUND Music
UPSOUND: (TRANSLATION:) Ek is hier by Mario Van Wyk se graf. (I am here at Mario Van Wyk’s grave.) En daar is baie, baie mense wat nie jou naam van vergeet nie. (And there are many people that won’t forget your name). Jy was in n baie goeie eenheid. (You were in a good unit.) Ons het saam julle gefight, ons was 61 Mech. (We fought together - we were 61 Mech.) “Wees asseblief met die mense wat agtergebly het, (Please be with those that are left behind - ) die families en almal wat hom onthou (- the families and everyone who remembers him).…wees asseblief met hulle tot einde van dae, amen.” (Please be with them until the end of days. Amen.)

VO15
In this final act….Eugene has found closure
pause
Christopher is carrying the history of his family forward to the next generation.
____________________________________________________________________

PROMOS

PROMO 1: 21 SECONDS
V/O In the furthest reaches of the globe, he found his roots
UPSOUND Christopher: My first ancestor was David Alexander Fitchet. In India he met his wife Mary Anne Collison, they got married at Fort William in Calcutta.

V/O Finding his ancestors connected him with his past
UPSOUND Christopher: I stumbled on the grave and I looked at the name and I thought to myself, you are the reason I am here.
___________________________________________________________________

PROMO 2: 21 SECONDS
V/O Overgrown with weeds and grass graves are buried in the past
UPSOUND Eugene: And then I go for it. Start walking, like bundu bashing. I’ve got a panga. I clean it as well as I can.

V/O Niche boxes vandalised and destroyed.
UPSOUND 08;49 in Bloemfontein where the memorial wall was, I stumbled among one of my ancestors' ashes lying on the floor.
_____________________________________________________________________

PROMO 3: 21 SECONDS:
V/O A veteran, haunted by the past
UPSOUND Eugene: When I go find a grave and there is another soldier, I don’t care what colour, what kind, whatever. His blood is red.

V/O… in search of closure he pays respect to the fallen.

UPSOUND Eugene: En daar’s baie, baie mense wat nie jou naam sal vergeet nie. SUBTITLES:
(And there are many people that won’t forget your name)

______________________________________________________________________

SUNDAY TEASER
Govan: Respecting the dead is about more than keeping our cemeteries clean….it is about preserving the identities of the people who are buried here…...
And now we tell the story of the people who are telling the stories of the dead, one photograph at a time.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 28 May 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: FINAL Script: Living Memory Duration: 10 minutes 22 seconds Date: 21 May 2025 INTRO SLOMO SHOTS UPSOUND CHRISTOPHER: You need to know where you come from in order to understand where you are going to…..And the starting point wasn’t with your birth. It goes back. UPSOUND EUGENE: When I go find a grave and there is another soldier, I don’t care what colour, what kind, whatever. Blood is red. LINK: There’s a story behind every grave, every tombstone…. It’s like opening a window into the past…you never know what you will find. VO1 We follow two very different people on their paths of discovery: A veteran from Gauteng, haunted by the ghosts of the Angola Border War…. and a family man from the Southern Cape with an intense longing to find his family roots. Christopher Fitchet: I started on this journey a couple of years ago to try and identify my ancestors and where they came from and at the time I didn’t realise the whirlwind romance relationship I would have with it. It has taken me to places I never thought I would never see. VO2 For Christopher Fitchet, the catalyst was the loss of his twins, born prematurely. Christopher Fitchet: Part of the problem was that we were not allowed to bury our children because of the legislation at the time, and that made me think well if there is no grave for them and there is a grave for me, their existence would never be known. They would remain unknown as though they never existed. VO3 A Grave is a sign that there was life and there was death…… For Eugene Liebenberg, it was the ghosts of the past that haunted him. Eugene Liebenberg: There’s about 2000 people that was killed in the border war, just on our side. LINK Between the 1960’s and 1990’s thousands of mostly white South Africans were conscripted to fight on the South African border…. You could defer it, but you couldn’t escape it. Up sound helicopter VO4 Unless they were conscientious objectors, all young men did compulsory military service. The Apartheid Government used conscription to combat threats of communism and African nationalism. Pause Eugene was only 18 when he was called up. He served in a unit under Operation Askari, a large-scale SADF operation into Angola to fight the military wing of the South West Africa People’s Orginasation, SWAPO and prevent a planned incursion into South West Africa. V/O 5 24 Soldiers died in Operation Askari ... .One of them was his friend, Corporal Johannes Hendrik Roets, known as Roetsie. Eugene Liebenberg: Man he was a kind ouk. He was one of the section leaders, he was nogal vris and he had a good sense of humour. Govan Whittles: Did you struggle to adjust to civilian life? Eugene Liebenberg: Unknowingly so. Because remember, all your buddies that didn’t go to the army were studying, were jolling. We were killing people. Govan Whittles: Jees… Eugene: You understand. Or you got killed. Get the bodies in body bags and ‘poef’, picked up by the chopper and they’re gone. And they get buried and whatever and we never see them again. VO6 After the war, Eugene closed himself off from the army - until one day he found himself at Roetsie’s grave in Thabazimbi. That was when his search of the graves of soldiers he knew began. Eugene: Something just fired me up, you understand, and I just went for it relentlessly. I just carried on in proper infantry style. I just went. VO7 In honour of their memory, Eugene cleaned the graves and sent the photos to the South Africa War Graves Project website where families can visit their loved ones on a virtual platform. Fade to black VO8 Christopher’s burning desire to find his ancestors took him to the far corners of the globe. Christopher Fitchet: My first ancestor was David Alexander Fitchet, he was born in Scotland and he was part of the 72nd royal regiment. They were part of the invasion of Blauberg against the Dutch government at the time at the Cape. Then he was sent to India. In India he then met his wife Mary Anne Collison, they got married at Fort William in Calcutta. VO9 It was in Fort William’s garrison in Calcutta that he found the marriage certificate of David Alexander Fitchet and Mary Ann Collison. Govan Whittles: Describe that moment where you researched someone on paper and found the cemetery where they’re buried. Did you find that connection that you wanted? Christopher Fitchet: Absolutely. Mary-ann Collison is as they say in Afrikaans the ‘stam moeder’ of all Fitchets in SA and she’s buried in Bedford cemetery in the Eastern Cape. And I stumbled on this grave and I looked at this name and I thought to myself, but YOU are the reason I am here. LINK When we think about family trees we think about commonality, the common ground that’s shared between all of us. But family trees are also about the stories that are unique to each person, to your mother, your father, your grandmother, great grandmother, even the ‘stam moeder’, and that’s what connects us. VO10 Christopher found 1500 Fitchets in the family tree….sadly some of their graves were badly neglected. Govan: What condition did you find the Bedford cemetery? Christopher: Overgrown, completely vandalised. In Bloemfontein for example I stumbled among one of my ancestors' ashes lying on the floor. I would say about 80% of the wall was completely vandalised, all the boxes were lying on the floor. We basically went puzzle building is what I called it where we tried to locate all the pieces that had been smashed and put them back together again. Ok you’re back there where you belong. VO11 A grave is a place of remembrance…a place to connect. Christopher Fitchet: I took my children to my grandparent’s graves….…there’s that connection. It's a sense of belonging. It's not about you and your parents and your children, that you actually belong to something a lot greater. VO12 These photographs may help others draw their family trees as well. Christopher has donated them to the Gravestone Photo Project, run by the Genealogical Society of South Africa. On this website, people can search for lost graves of their loved ones. Riana Le Roux: Many of the cemeteries are not accessible any more and they are being destroyed so we will have a photograph at least for posterity, some sort of record of the person who was buried there, many burial records disappear. VO13 Riana le Roux has been cataloguing over one million photographs taken by volunteers like Chrstopher to serve as a national asset for families in search of family graves. Govan Whittles: How did you get involved in the project? Riana le Roux: Coordinator: Gravestone Photo Project - As a child we used to go to the Westpark cemetery quite often. It was a family tradition, Christmas Day. As I grew older I never lost my love for cemeteries. A lot of us, especially genealogists, we just love cemeteries. Govan Whittles: Why do you think people are interested in genealogy? Riana le Roux: Personally I think it is nice to know your roots where you came from. I find people who are, people for instance who are adopted, there is always a question, who am I? Where did I come from, where do I belong? So I think genealogy gives you the answers. UP SOUND MUSIC VO14 Finding the graves of fallen soldiers has brought back powerful memories for Eugene ….today will be his last. UPSOUND: Govan Whittles: I cant’ believe how overgrown this place is. Eugene Liebenberg: It’s unreal Govan ... .very, very, sad hey. Govan Whittles: Do you come here alone? Eugene Liebenberg: No not always hey. This youngster, my ‘handskind’, came with me and he helped me find about 9 graves over the years and then he does the spanner work. We share it a bit. Govan (laughs) Eugene: Yeah. Govan: Lekker hey. Eugene: He also plays the bagpipes. Govan: The bagpipes? Eugene: Yeah. UPSOUND Music UPSOUND: (TRANSLATION:) Ek is hier by Mario Van Wyk se graf. (I am here at Mario Van Wyk’s grave.) En daar is baie, baie mense wat nie jou naam van vergeet nie. (And there are many people that won’t forget your name). Jy was in n baie goeie eenheid. (You were in a good unit.) Ons het saam julle gefight, ons was 61 Mech. (We fought together - we were 61 Mech.) “Wees asseblief met die mense wat agtergebly het, (Please be with those that are left behind - ) die families en almal wat hom onthou (- the families and everyone who remembers him).…wees asseblief met hulle tot einde van dae, amen.” (Please be with them until the end of days. Amen.) metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Meet two rather unusual people: Christopher Fitchet from the Southern Cape and Eugene Liebenberg from Gauteng, both paying homage to the dead by visiting their graves.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Christopher had a burning desire to trace the origin of his rather unusual family name and Eugene, still haunted by the ghosts of the border war, to pay homage to the fallen brothers in arms.
metadata.Summary: Christopher Fitchet’s mission began 8 years ago when he searched for his ancestors. Even though the surname is uncommon, few documents were available on the family tree. He turned to the cemeteries across the country in the hope of finding family graves: his search took him from the Eastern Cape to the Free State and all the way down to the Western Cape, photographing every single Fitchet gravestone and documenting the family tree. It turned out there were 1500 South African family members with that surname (Pretorius is about 200 000 in comparison). He traced his founding mother, Mary-Anne Collison, born in England and his Founding father from Calcutta who ended up in South Africa when their ship landed in the Cape in 1817. During this mission to document the graves of the ancestors he noticed the state of neglect of the graves in cemeteries across the country and that is ‘when the penny dropped’ said Christopher. I had to photograph every single grave in the cemetery as a method of preserving the dead as tomorrow it might not be there any more. In some instances the burial register is gone which means if the graves are destroyed the dead will forever disappear in living history. From the caretakers he heard stories of people removing the headstones to sell, others were digging for jewelry in the boxes as they believe it is buried with the deceased, and the worst is stealing the ashes of the dead to mix with street drugs like Nyaope. In Bloemfontein he spent 4 days picking up ashes and putting the memorial plaques back again - including those of his family buried there. Christopher’s passion to preserve the history of the dead has resulted in over 350 000 photos taken of the graves in many towns, cities and even on farms. The photos are then donated to the Genealogical Society of South Africa’s Gravestone Photos Project and available on their website for anyone searching for a family member. There are a number of organisations focusing on documenting graves, but none were focusing on the rural areas and the farms so this became his focus over the last 3 years. For Christopher this is a way of giving back because life is not just about taking, he says. Over the years he has met very interesting people and places like Uniondale known for its ghost of a lonely young woman who hitches a ride and then when people offer her a lift, she gets into the car and then simply vanishes. The ghost, known as Maria Roux, was a young woman who tragically died in the early hours of 12 April 1968 when her fiance lost control of the car in which they were travelling. He visited the farm nearby the exact place where the accident happened and it was a strange eerie feeling, he remembered. Christopher’s next photographic grave project is Swellendam in the Western Cape, a historic town established in 1745 named after Governor Hendrik Swellengrebel and his wife Helena ten DammeIt. There are over 50 provincial heritage sites, 4 cemeteries, and a large number of farm graves in the district. Eugene Liebenberg’s story is rather different: Having fought in the border war he pays homage to the fallen soldiers in Operation Askari and Operation Sceptic, also known as Operation Smokeshell. He finds the grave sites from the records on the South African War Graves project, whose aim is to archive photographs from South African and Rhodesian wars. He then locates the graves to pay homage. He found most of the soldiers’ graves neglected, overgrown and unsafe to visit. “Some graves, like the ones in Boksburg cemetery, are so overgrown that I spend hours clearing my way through the weeds in search of the graves”, says Eugene. “It takes hours sometimes and I can’t believe that no-one cuts the lawn and keeps the place clean”, says Eugene. After clearing the site around the grave, Eugene cleans the dust from the headstone and places a small bunch of flowers on the grave as an act of respect and remembrance. He then takes a moment of silence to remember the fallen soldier. In a symbolic act of honouring the soldier and their journey in the afterlife he drinks a toast to angels as a way of acknowledging their presence in the world of spirits and offering respect to their guardian angel. Eugene has struggled to come to terms with the war he had a part in - not of his own choice - and this he feels is a way of finding peace and remembering the brothers who did not make it alive, says Eugene. For Eugene it is a matter of finding closure on a war he did not choose, paying his last respect. For Christopher every roadtrip to a forgotten cemetery on a farm or a town or a hamlet is a journey back into the past where he painstakingly captures frame by frame a tombstone of a family member creating a “window to the past”, etched in memory. And for those who cannot get to the graves, being able to see their loved ones' burial site online is a special feeling, says Christopher. Riana Le Roux manages the Photographic Grave Project on the Genealogical Society of South Africa’s website. She spent a decade cataloguing and posting hundreds of thousands of photographs from graves in South Africa and neighbouring countries on the website for viewers to find at the click of a button. The search engine is easy to navigate. All graves that have been photographed and sent to Riana will be available online. By simply entering the name and surname of a loved one and the province where the person was buried, the photo of the grave and exact location will be displayed on the screen. “We are constantly updating our site and are thankful for people like Christopher who dedicate their spare time on taking photos for those who cannot get to the grave, and some people who live far away and are not able to go to the cemetery to pay respect”, says Riana. We will conduct a zoom interview with Riana who lives in Baberton; spend a day with Eugene in Boksburg at the local cemetery and a day with Chrisotopher at cemeteries in Swellendam. In addition we have graves from cemeteries in the Northern Cape and Ceres, taken by our cameraman when he travelled through that area. ADDITIONAL VISUALS: Photos from Eugene in his army days; photos from an ex soldier who served on the border and kindly made his own photos available; plus 50 seconds of licensed film footage, purchased from Peter Lamberti, a professional filmmaker, to ‘set the mood’ of the Border War. On the Fitchet family, we have photographs of the graves Christopher managed to find plus a family tree graphic to illustrate the genealogy and family line dating back to the ‘Stam moeder” / matriarch. All photos on the Photographic War Project is available for us to download. ________________________________________________________________________________________________
